This reference gives one agreed meaning for each concept the twelve chapters of
Part Two use. It exists so that a reader who meets a term in Chapter 3 can find
the chapter and section that explains it, and so that the chapters need not
define a term again each time they use it. The concept tables gather
related terms into broad groups and give each term's meaning or essential
distinction; the closing table records the notation the chapters share. It is
written for lookup rather than for reading through. Chapters 1--4 are
available on the website; references to Chapters 5--12 point forward to
chapters that are not yet available.

A row is read from left to right. The preferred name comes first, with the
common alternatives a reader will meet elsewhere beside it. The meaning cell
states the essential distinction rather than a full explanation. The final cell
of a concept table, **Main explanation**, is a destination: the chapter and
section where the term is principally explained, with a first use elsewhere
noted where one exists. In the notation table the **Main use** column carries
that destination and a further column records alternative symbols and the
cautions attached to them. Terms that name the same concept in context share an
entry, related concepts with different meanings have separate entries, and a
symbol whose preferred form carries a qualifier takes a row of its own that
names its other uses. This reference records the vocabulary rather than
teaching it: first-use explanations, worked examples and the reasons behind each
distinction stay in the chapters themselves.

\small

## Latent Variables and the Common-Factor Model {#sec-p2-concepts-latent .unnumbered}

| Concept group | Term and common alternatives | Meaning or essential distinction | Main explanation |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Latent-variable modeling | Latent variable (common factor, $\eta_k$) | An unobserved random variable introduced by a model and given a distribution over units. It is not a parameter, not a score, and not made observable by being named. | Chapter 1, Sec. 1.1 |
| Latent-variable modeling | Construct | A substantive idea in the research question. Its meaning comes from theory, item content, response processes, population and intended use, none of which a covariance matrix supplies. | Chapter 1, Sec. 1.1 |
| Latent-variable modeling | Indicator (item, observed response $Y_j$) | An observed variable proposed to bear on a factor; an item response is the value recorded for one unit. | Chapter 1, Sec. 1.1 |
| Latent-variable modeling | Domain sampling (content or behavioral domain coverage) | Defensible coverage of the domain a construct names. It supports a broad construct interpretation and is usually systematic rather than a literal probability sample; it is a different question from sampling units from a population. | Chapter 1, Sec. 1.1 |
| Latent-variable modeling | Reflective direction (formative alternative) | The modelling choice that writes each indicator as a function of the factors plus a residual. It states a direction of representation, not a causal finding, and it fails for constructs whose indicators produce them. | Chapter 1, Sec. 1.1 |
| Latent-variable modeling | Classical true score ($X_{ir}=T_i+E_{ir}$) | The expected score of a person over repetitions of a specified procedure. It is a property of a person and a procedure, so a stable irrelevant influence stays inside it; it equals a common factor only under added assumptions. | Chapter 1, Sec. 1.2 |
| Common-factor model | Common-factor model (linear factor model) | $\mathbf y_i=\boldsymbol\nu+\boldsymbol\Lambda\boldsymbol\eta_i+\boldsymbol\epsilon_i$ with the moment assumptions on $\boldsymbol\eta_i$ and $\boldsymbol\epsilon_i$. Its predictors are not columns of the dataset, which is what separates it from a regression. | Chapter 1, Sec. 2.1--2.2 |
| Common-factor model | Loading (pattern coefficient, $\lambda_{jk}$) | A fixed unknown parameter relating indicator $j$ to factor $k$ on a chosen factor metric. It is not a person's score and not a direct measure of how much attribute a person has. | Chapter 1, Sec. 2.1 |
| Common-factor model | Residual (unique part, $\epsilon_j$) and residual covariance $\theta_{jk}$ | The part of an indicator the declared factors do not represent, which may hold random fluctuation, item-specific content, method or occasion effects, an omitted factor, or misspecification. A residual covariance is a pair-specific relation outside the common part. | Chapter 1, Sec. 2.3 |
| Common-factor model | Factor covariance matrix ($\boldsymbol\Phi$) | The $m\times m$ variance-covariance matrix of the factors, symmetric and positive semidefinite. It is total latent covariance, distinct from a disturbance covariance in a later structural model. | Chapter 1, Sec. 2.2 |
| Common-factor model | Local independence (conditional independence) | Indicators being independent given the factors. It is stronger than zero conditional residual covariance, which is stronger than the zero unconditional covariance a diagonal $\boldsymbol\Theta$ supplies; none of the three says the observed items are unrelated. | Chapter 1, Sec. 2.3 |
| Specification | Simple structure and cross-loading | A loading pattern in which each indicator relates to one factor, the remaining entries being fixed at zero; a cross-loading is a nonzero entry outside that pattern. Each zero is a restriction, not a drawing convenience. As a rotation criterion the same pattern favours relatively few substantial relations per item and identifiable indicator groups; it is not a criterion of fit to the observed covariance matrix, and rotation does not improve $F_{\mathrm{ML}}$. | Chapter 1, Sec. 3.1; as a rotation criterion Chapter 2, Sec. 5.2 |
| Specification | Fixed, free and constrained parameter (parameter restriction) | Three distinct statuses an entry of $\boldsymbol\Lambda$, $\boldsymbol\Phi$ or $\boldsymbol\Theta$ can hold: fixed at a declared value, freely estimated, or tied to another parameter. A path diagram does not distinguish them. | Chapter 1, Sec. 3.2 |
| Factor scale | Scale setting (marker variable, fixed factor) | Supplying a metric to a factor that has none, either by fixing one loading per factor or by fixing the factor variance. Neither convention is superior, and the implied covariance among indicators is the same under both. | Chapter 1, Sec. 4.1 |
| Factor scale | Sign indeterminacy | Reversing a factor's direction and every one of its loadings leaves every product, and therefore the implied covariance, unchanged. A negative sign is a convention, and a sign flip between equivalent solutions is not a change in results. | Chapter 1, Sec. 4.2 |
| Factor scale | Location convention (latent intercept $\boldsymbol\alpha$) | Fixing the origin of the factors, usually by setting the single-group factor means at zero, because observed means cannot determine unrestricted intercepts and unrestricted factor means together. $\boldsymbol\alpha$ is a latent intercept and coincides with $E(\boldsymbol\eta_i)$ only without structural paths. | Chapter 1, Sec. 4.2 |
| Factor scale | Observed-unit change | Re-expressing recorded indicators in different units, which changes loadings, residual variances and implied covariances coherently and predictably. Nothing is indeterminate; this is not a latent-coordinate convention. | Chapter 1, Sec. 4.3 |
| Factor scale | Rotational freedom (coordinate change, $\mathbf Q$) | The freedom, with two or more factors, to replace the axes while corresponding changes to $\boldsymbol\Lambda$ and $\boldsymbol\Phi$ leave the observed covariance unchanged. It resolves a representation choice and establishes nothing substantive. | Chapter 1, Sec. 4.1 and 7 |
| Covariance structure | Model-implied covariance $\boldsymbol\Sigma(\boldsymbol\vartheta)$ (covariance structure analysis) | $\boldsymbol\Lambda\boldsymbol\Phi\boldsymbol\Lambda^{\mathsf T}+\boldsymbol\Theta$: the covariance the model implies, split into a common and a residual part. It needs finite second moments and the stated moment restrictions, not normality. | Chapter 1, Sec. 5 |
| Covariance structure | Pattern matrix and structure matrix ($\boldsymbol\Lambda\boldsymbol\Phi$) | $\boldsymbol\Lambda$ holds the coefficients of the indicator equations; $\boldsymbol\Lambda\boldsymbol\Phi$ holds indicator-factor covariances. They coincide under orthogonal unit-variance factors and must be read side by side in an oblique solution. | Chapter 1, Sec. 5; oblique reading Chapter 2, Sec. 6.1 |
| Covariance structure | Communality ($h_j^{2}$) | The common part of an indicator's variance, $\boldsymbol\lambda_j^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\Phi\boldsymbol\lambda_j$, under the declared model. The shortcut $\lambda_j^{2}$ holds only for one nonzero loading on a unit-variance factor; correlated factors add a cross term. | Chapter 1, Sec. 5.1 |
| Covariance structure | Uniqueness (residual variance; Heywood case) | $\theta_{jj}=1-h_j^{2}$ for a standardized indicator: variance the declared common factors do not represent, which is not the same as random error. A negative estimate is an improper, or Heywood, solution. | Chapter 1, Sec. 5.1 |
| Covariance structure | Moment structure ($\boldsymbol\mu(\boldsymbol\vartheta)$) | The modeled object is the mean and covariance pair; $\boldsymbol\mu=\boldsymbol\nu+\boldsymbol\Lambda\boldsymbol\alpha$. Analysing covariances alone sets the mean structure aside, which is a choice rather than an absence. | Chapter 1, Sec. 5.2 |
| Covariance structure | Distinct moment and degrees of freedom ($u=p(p+1)/2$, $df=u-t$) | The number of distinct entries a covariance matrix supplies, and its difference from the free-parameter count. More respondents estimate the same moments more precisely; $df\ge0$ is necessary for, and never proof of, identification. | Chapter 1, Sec. 5.3 |
| Covariance structure | Tetrad restriction | The vanishing of $\sigma_{jk}\sigma_{lm}-\sigma_{jm}\sigma_{lk}$, which one common factor with uncorrelated residuals forces for every four indicators. A nonzero tetrad refutes exact reproduction by that model, whatever its loadings. | Chapter 1, Sec. 6.3 |
| Covariance structure | SS loading (column sum of squared loadings) | A summary of one factor column across indicators, read after rotation as a column statistic of the oriented solution. It is not in general an eigenvalue of the analysed correlation matrix, the matrix being decomposed must always be named, and with correlated factors it gives no unique additive partition of common variance. | Chapter 1, Sec. 6.1; post-rotation reading Chapter 2, Sec. 3.2 |
| Neighboring objects | Factor-score estimate ($\widehat{\eta}_{ik}$) | A prediction of an unobserved factor value from responses, a fitted model and a scoring rule. Different rules give different numbers from the same fit, and no rule makes it an error-free measurement. | Chapter 1, Sec. 6.5 |
| Neighboring objects | Principal component and prespecified composite | Weighted composites of observed variables, one chosen to capture observed variance and one declared as a rule such as a sum or mean. Neither decomposes covariance into common and residual parts, so neither answers the common-factor model's question. | Chapter 1, Sec. 6.5 |
| Analytic orientation | Exploratory, confirmatory and hybrid orientation | Names for how much is declared before the focal analysis, not for unrelated models. Both use the same covariance decomposition; the restrictions and the history of the decisions separate them. | Chapter 1, Sec. 1.4 and 6.6 |
| Analytic orientation | Analytic status (development versus confirmation evidence) | The record of which body of evidence informed each decision. A specification chosen on one body of evidence receives a genuinely new test only from evidence not used to choose it; analyses move from confirmatory to exploratory status and never back. | Chapter 1, Sec. 6.6--6.7 |

: Latent variables and the common-factor model. {#tbl-intro-p2-concepts-latent tbl-colwidths="[16,23,45,16]"}

## Exploratory Factor Analysis and Model Development {#sec-p2-concepts-efa .unnumbered}

| Concept group | Term and common alternatives | Meaning or essential distinction | Main explanation |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Exploratory analysis | Exploratory factor analysis (EFA) | A common-factor analysis that leaves most loading restrictions open while seeking a comparatively low-dimensional representation of shared covariation. It is not assumption-free: the indicator set, population, association matrix, residual restriction, dimensional range and rotation criterion all shape what it can reveal. | Chapter 2, Sec. 1 |
| Exploratory analysis | Development sample (development record) | The sample whose inspection produces a model. A model developed after inspecting these observations is exploratory with respect to them whatever fitting function is used, so the same records cannot confirm it. | Chapter 2, Sec. 1 |
| Extraction | Squared multiple correlation (SMC) | For indicator $j$, the $R^2$ from regressing it on all other indicators, computed as $1-1/(\mathbf R^{-1})_{jj}$. It is a regression summary of the observed matrix used as a communality start, not a known common variance. | Chapter 2, Sec. 2.3 |
| Extraction | Reduced correlation matrix (SMC-reduced matrix) | The correlation matrix with communality estimates replacing the unit diagonal. It need not be positive semidefinite, and its eigenvalues are on a different scale from the full matrix's. | Chapter 2, Sec. 2.3 |
| Extraction | Principal-axis factoring (PAF) | Iterative extraction that decomposes a reduced matrix, forms loadings from its leading positive roots and updates the diagonal from row sums of squared loadings. The diagonal start, nonpositive-root handling and stopping rule are implementation choices. | Chapter 2, Sec. 2.3 |
| Extraction | Minimum-residual extraction (minres) | Extraction minimizing the sum of squared off-diagonal correlation residuals, giving each displayed discrepancy equal weight. It is a common-factor method but not another name for PAF. | Chapter 2, Sec. 2.4 |
| Retention | Kaiser--Guttman rule (eigenvalue-greater-than-one) | Retaining roots above one in a unit-diagonal correlation analysis. Sampling variation alone produces roots above one, and applying the threshold to a reduced matrix changes the comparison. | Chapter 2, Sec. 3.3 |
| Retention | Scree plot | An ordered plot of eigenvalues read for where large decreases give way to a flatter sequence. It supplies no sampling reference, and full- and reduced-matrix plots need not agree. | Chapter 2, Sec. 3.3 |
| Retention | Parallel analysis (permutation parallel analysis) | Comparing each observed eigenvalue with the same-rank eigenvalues of datasets built to have no common factors but the same sample size and marginal distributions, and retaining the leading consecutive run that clears its reference. The eigenvalue basis, the null generator, the reference statistic and the replication count and seed all belong to the specification. | Chapter 2, Sec. 3.4 |
| Retention | Empirical Kaiser criterion (EKC) | A sample-adjusted repair of Kaiser--Guttman using the Marchenko--Pastur bound $(1+\sqrt{p/n})^2$ for the first root, correcting later roots for variance already accounted for and flooring the reference at one. | Chapter 2, Sec. 3.5 |
| Retention | Sequential model tests | Fitting successive factor counts and stopping at the first non-significant exact-fit test. The sequence is trustworthy only while still under-fitting, because the $\chi^2$ reference fails once the count exceeds the true number. | Chapter 2, Sec. 3.5 |
| Retention | Combination rule | Using two criteria with different references together, and treating their disagreement as evidence that the dimensions are hard to detect rather than as a tie to be broken by vote. | Chapter 2, Sec. 3.5 |
| Counting | Effective EFA parameter count ($t_m$) | $pm+p-m(m-1)/2$ for an unrestricted common-factor covariance model at regular points, with $df_m=p(p+1)/2-t_m$. The subtraction removes rotational redundancy; an oblique rotation adds no parameters because it re-expresses the same fitted covariance. | Chapter 2, Sec. 4.1 |
| Counting | Ledermann bound | The largest factor count the covariance moments can generically support, $m\le(2p+1-\sqrt{8p+1})/2$. It is a counting limit, not a recommendation, a positive-root count or a proof of identification. | Chapter 2, Sec. 4.1 |
| Rotation | Inverse-paired transformation | The general nonsingular change of factor coordinates $\boldsymbol\Lambda\mathbf T^{-1}$ with $\mathbf T\boldsymbol\Phi\mathbf T^{\mathsf T}$, which leaves the fitted common covariance unchanged. Multiplying loadings while leaving $\boldsymbol\Phi$ alone is not an equivalent oblique rotation. | Chapter 2, Sec. 5.1 |
| Rotation | Varimax | An orthogonal criterion maximizing the dispersion of squared loadings within columns. A clean varimax pattern does not establish that the substantive attributes are unrelated. | Chapter 2, Sec. 5.2 |
| Rotation | Direct oblimin (quartimin at $\gamma=0$) | An oblique criterion discouraging large squared coefficients in several columns of one row while permitting factor correlations. The name alone is not a specification: $\gamma$, normalization, tolerance, iteration limit, starts and seed all matter. | Chapter 2, Sec. 5.2 |
| Rotation | Kaiser normalization | Dividing each loading row by its communality-based length before optimizing and restoring the scale afterward, which reweights indicators in the criterion. It is not the same operation as standardizing the observed variables. | Chapter 2, Sec. 5.2 |
| Reading an oblique solution | Pattern coefficient (pattern matrix $\mathbf P$) | The coefficient of a factor in the simultaneous decomposition of a standardized indicator, read conditional on the other factors in the same representation. | Chapter 2, Sec. 6.1 |
| Reading an oblique solution | Structure correlation (structure matrix $\mathbf C=\mathbf P\boldsymbol\Phi$) | The zero-order indicator--factor correlation, which can be appreciable where the pattern coefficient is near zero because part of the relation travels through the factor correlation. Pattern and structure coincide only in an orthogonal solution. | Chapter 2, Sec. 6.1 (defined as $\boldsymbol\Lambda\boldsymbol\Phi$ in Chapter 1, Sec. 5) |
| Reading an oblique solution | Oblique communality as a quadratic form | $h_j^2=\mathbf p_j^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\Phi\mathbf p_j$, whose factor-correlation cross-products are part of the common variance. A row sum of squared pattern coefficients omits them and is a different quantity. | Chapter 2, Sec. 6.2 |
| Residual evidence | Correlation residual matrix ($\mathbf E$) and off-diagonal RMS | Observed minus reproduced correlations, summarized by $\sqrt{2\sum_{j<k}e_{jk}^2/[p(p-1)]}$, which excludes variances. The largest absolute residual and the location of discrepancy carry information an average conceals, and this summary is not automatically any software statistic named RMSR or SRMR. | Chapter 2, Sec. 7.1 |
| Residual evidence | Uniqueness boundary (bound-constrained uniqueness) | A fitted uniqueness at the implementation's lower bound rather than in the interior. It can signal too many factors, a redundant pair, sampling fluctuation or misspecification, and is different evidence from an interior estimate. | Chapter 2, Sec. 4.3 |
| Preliminary summaries | KMO (Kaiser--Meyer--Olkin measure of sampling adequacy) | The ratio of summed squared zero-order correlations to that sum plus the summed squared partial correlations. It describes the input; it selects no factor count and is no minimum-sample-size calculation. | Chapter 2, Sec. 7.2 |
| Preliminary summaries | Bartlett's test of sphericity | A normal-theory test of $H_0:\mathbf R_{\mathrm{population}}=\mathbf I$ on $p(p-1)/2$ df. Rejection says the indicators are not mutually uncorrelated, not that a low-dimensional factor model fits. | Chapter 2, Sec. 7.2 |
| Analytic sensitivity | Tucker's congruence coefficient | The cosine between two loading-column vectors, compared after column order and sign are aligned. It compares coefficient directions, not participant scores, and near-one congruence can hide an important difference for one item. | Chapter 2, Sec. 7.3 |
| Analytic sensitivity | Analytic sensitivity comparison | Changing one declared analytic choice at a time on the same records and comparing aligned solutions. It is same-sample evidence about analytic robustness, never an independent replication or a sampling interval. | Chapter 2, Sec. 7.3 |
| Analytic status | Frozen candidate specification | The exact item order, free and fixed relations, scaling, covariance and mean settings, estimation family and named rivals recorded before any confirmation evidence is inspected. This separates a planned confirmation from a comparison developed after inspection, whose interpretation must acknowledge that selection. | Chapter 2, Sec. 8 |
| Analytic status | Planned rival model | A restriction or broader alternative named before the confirmation outcome, distinguished from a post-hoc change, which changes analytic status and requires new evidence. | Chapter 2, Sec. 8 |

: Exploratory factor analysis and model development. {#tbl-intro-p2-concepts-efa tbl-colwidths="[16,23,45,16]"}

## Confirmatory Specification, Identification, and Estimation {#sec-p2-concepts-cfa .unnumbered}

| Concept group | Term and common alternatives | Meaning or essential distinction | Main explanation |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Confirmatory specification | Confirmatory factor analysis (restricted factor model; CFA) | A common-factor model whose loading, residual, and factor-covariance entries are restricted before estimation, giving testable implications beyond the number of factors. The label describes restrictions and analytic history, not a favorable conclusion or a function name. | Chapter 3, Sec. 1 |
| Confirmatory specification | Exclusion restriction (fixed zero loading; absent arrow) | A loading entry set to zero as a substantive claim that the indicator has no direct relation to that factor. It does not state that the indicator and factor are uncorrelated, because correlated factors still induce a nonzero structure coefficient. | Chapter 3, Sec. 1 |
| Parameter status | Free, fixed, equality-constrained, bounded, and defined parameter | Estimated under the other restrictions; assigned a constant; required to share a value; restricted to a range; or computed from fitted parameters without adding freedom. A diagram shows which relations exist, not which status each has. | Chapter 3, Sec. 3 |
| Parameter status | Residual covariance (correlated residual; correlated uniqueness) | A freely estimated off-diagonal entry of $\boldsymbol\Theta$, occupying two symmetric cells and adding one free parameter. It changes one indicator pair's implied covariance, unlike a cross-loading, which changes a whole row and column. | Chapter 3, Sec. 3 |
| Latent metric | Marker scaling (reference indicator; unit loading identification) | Fixing one loading per factor at one, so the factor is expressed in that indicator's units and the factor variance is estimated. It does not set the factor variance to one and does not make the marker error-free. | Chapter 3, Sec. 4 |
| Latent metric | Fixed-factor scaling (unit variance identification; `std.lv = TRUE`) | Fixing each factor variance at one and estimating every target loading, so a factor unit is one model standard deviation in a single-group model. It does not standardize the observed indicators. | Chapter 3, Sec. 4 |
| Latent metric | Factor-scale reparameterization ($\mathbf D$ transformation) | The diagonal rescaling $\boldsymbol\Lambda^*=\boldsymbol\Lambda\mathbf D^{-1}$, $\boldsymbol\Phi^*=\mathbf D\boldsymbol\Phi\mathbf D^{\mathsf T}$, which leaves the implied covariance and $\boldsymbol\Theta$ unchanged. Equivalence fails if a constraint is not transformed with the metric or a factor variance is on a boundary. | Chapter 3, Sec. 4 |
| Observed units | Observed-unit rescaling ($\boldsymbol\Delta$ rescaling) | Replacing $\mathbf y$ by $\mathbf b+\boldsymbol\Delta\mathbf y$, which multiplies an indicator's intercept and loading by its factor, its variance and residual variance by that factor squared, and its covariance with an unchanged indicator by the factor. It changes the record, not the latent coordinates, and leaves fit unchanged under a consistently transformed model. | Chapter 3, Sec. 4 |
| Observed units | Correlation reparameterization (standardized-indicator model) | Writing $\mathbf R=\mathbf D_y^{-1/2}\boldsymbol\Sigma\mathbf D_y^{-1/2}$ with rescaled loading and residual matrices. It standardizes the indicators, not the factors, and its moment count differs from the covariance form because the unit diagonal is fixed. | Chapter 3, Sec. 4 |
| Coefficient metrics | Latent-standardized and fully standardized loading (`std.lv`; `std.all`) | $\lambda\sqrt{\phi_{aa}}$ expresses a factor change in standard-deviation units in the indicator's raw unit; $\lambda\sqrt{\phi_{aa}}/\sqrt{\sigma_{jj}}$ standardizes both. A raw standard error is not the standardized coefficient's standard error, because the transformation uses estimated quantities. | Chapter 3, Sec. 4 |
| Moment accounting | Observed moments, free parameters, and model degrees of freedom ($u$, $t$, $df=u-t$) | The distinct sample moments a declared representation supplies, the free coordinates the model estimates, and their difference. Necessary bookkeeping for one stated representation; neither identification nor quality, and unique covariance entries are not observations. | Chapter 3, Sec. 6 |
| Moment accounting | Unrestricted-EFA dimension | The count of distinct covariance-model axes in an unrestricted $m$-factor solution, $pm+p-m(m-1)/2$ at regular full-rank points, which subtracts the continuous rotational freedom that changes the display without changing the reproduced covariance. | Chapter 3, Sec. 6 |
| Identification | Identification (global, local, and generic; empirical or weak identification) | Whether the moments determine the parameters: uniquely over the admissible space, in a neighborhood, or except at exceptional values. Weak identification describes a recoverable model whose parameters are poorly distinguished, showing as unstable estimates and very large standard errors rather than an error message. | Chapter 3, Sec. 6 |
| Identification | Two- and three-indicator sufficient conditions (connectedness) | A factor with at least three exclusive indicators is identified under a fixed scale and diagonal residuals; a factor with two exclusive indicators needs a nonzero covariance with another identified factor. Both are sufficient and neither is necessary, and the second depends on an estimated quantity. | Chapter 3, Sec. 6 |
| Identification | Moment Jacobian rank check | Full column rank of $\partial\mathbf s/\partial\boldsymbol\vartheta^{\mathsf T}$ at a regular fitted point, a local diagnostic that supports local identification. It does not prove global uniqueness or uniform stability, and it is a check on the fitted solution rather than a structural proof. | Chapter 3, Sec. 6 |
| Model relations | Nested, nonnested, and equivalent models (observational equivalence) | Nesting requires that every covariance matrix one model generates belongs to the other's set, shown by the restrictions producing the inclusion. Equal degrees of freedom imply neither nesting nor equivalence, and observational equivalence limits what covariance data can distinguish. | Chapter 3, Sec. 6 |
| Estimation | Normal-theory ML discrepancy ($F_{\mathrm{ML}}$) | $\log|\boldsymbol\Sigma(\boldsymbol\vartheta)|+\operatorname{tr}\{\mathbf S\boldsymbol\Sigma(\boldsymbol\vartheta)^{-1}\}-\log|\mathbf S|-p$, minimized over the admissible parameter space and normalized to zero at $\boldsymbol\Sigma=\mathbf S$. The covariance equation needs no normality; the conventional standard errors and test do. | Chapter 3, Sec. 7 (first used Chapter 2, Sec. 2.4) |
| Estimation | Covariance divisor convention ($\mathbf S_N$ against $\mathbf S_{N-1}$; normal against Wishart) | $\mathbf S_N=\{(N-1)/N\}\mathbf S_{N-1}$ is the normal-likelihood convention; the Wishart convention uses an $N-1$ covariance and multiplier. A supplied covariance matrix communicates neither the sample size nor the divisor, so the convention must be disclosed and never applied twice. | Chapter 3, Sec. 7 |
| Mean structure | Indicator intercepts and the latent location convention | Free indicator intercepts with latent intercepts fixed at zero add $p$ moments and $p$ parameters, leaving the covariance restrictions and degrees of freedom unchanged. Freeing both at once identifies no latent origin, because $\boldsymbol\alpha+\mathbf c$ with $\boldsymbol\nu-\boldsymbol\Lambda\mathbf c$ reproduces the same means. | Chapter 3, Sec. 5 |
| Solution quality | Convergence, admissibility, and the Heywood case | Convergence is an optimizer's stopping statement; admissibility requires positive residual variances and positive definite factor and implied covariance matrices. A negative or zero residual variance is a symptom of the whole decomposition and is neither a cosmetic warning nor something to replace by zero in a report. | Chapter 3, Sec. 8 |
| Inference | Wald test of a linear restriction ($\mathbf R\boldsymbol\vartheta=\mathbf r$) | A $\chi^2_q$ test computed from the estimates and their covariance matrix, requiring the covariance between estimates and not only their variances. It tests the stated restriction conditional on the rest of the model; it is not a global-fit test and need not equal a refitted likelihood-ratio statistic. | Chapter 3, Sec. 8 |
| Transition record | Evaluation transition record (handoff record) | The auditable record of evidence identity, model, parameter conventions, estimation settings, numerical checks, parameter uncertainty, global/local evaluation and its limits, and reproduction metadata. It preserves what was fixed, inspected, or revised so a later comparison cannot silently change the analysis. | Chapter 3, Sec. 8 |
| Observed system | Parceling (item aggregation) | Fitting $\mathbf z=\mathbf A\mathbf y$ with $\operatorname{Var}(\mathbf z)=\mathbf A\boldsymbol\Sigma\mathbf A^{\mathsf T}$. Reducing dimension lets different item-level patterns give the same parcel covariance, so a well-fitting parcel model does not establish the item-level restrictions. | Chapter 3, Appendix |

: Confirmatory specification, identification, and estimation. {#tbl-intro-p2-concepts-cfa tbl-colwidths="[16,23,45,16]"}

\Needspace{18\baselineskip}

## Evaluation, Comparison, Reliability, and Extensions {#sec-p2-concepts-evaluation .unnumbered}

| Concept group | Term and common alternatives | Meaning or essential distinction | Main explanation |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Global fit | Model chi-square (exact-fit test; likelihood-ratio model test) | $T_M=N\widehat F_{\mathrm{ML}}$ referred to $\chi^2_{df_M}$, testing whether some admissible parameter vector reproduces the population moment structure exactly. Nonrejection is not acceptance of the model, and rejection at large $N$ is evidence against exact fit rather than a measure of its magnitude. | Chapter 3, Sec. 8; Chapter 4, Sec. 2 |
| Global fit | RMSEA (root mean square error of approximation) with its 90% interval | Estimated discrepancy per degree of freedom, $\sqrt{\max\{(T_M-df_M)/(N\,df_M),0\}}$, whose behavior also depends on model size and degrees of freedom, with an interval obtained by inverting a noncentral chi-square reference. A zero estimate is a truncation, not zero residuals; the convention ($N$ or $N-1$) must be named. | Chapter 3, Sec. 8; Chapter 4, Sec. 2 |
| Global fit | Incremental fit index (CFI; TLI or NNFI) with its independence baseline | Improvement of the model relative to a stated reference rather than relative to exact fit. The usual baseline frees the observed variances and fixes all covariances to zero, so a high value depends on how poor that baseline is; TLI is not bounded by one. | Chapter 3, Sec. 8; Chapter 4, Sec. 2 |
| Global fit | SRMR (standardized root mean square residual) | Root mean square of observed-SD-standardized covariance residuals over one triangle including the diagonal. Not a mean absolute residual; a small value can hide a few large cells among many near-zero ones. | Chapter 3, Sec. 8; Chapter 4, Sec. 3 |
| Local diagnosis | Covariance residual (raw; observed-SD-standardized; correlation residual) | Observed minus implied covariance, either in the product of the two indicators' units, divided by the product of observed SDs, or as a difference of separately formed correlations. None is a residual divided by its sampling standard error, so none is automatically a $z$ statistic. | Chapter 3, Sec. 8; Chapter 4, Sec. 3 |
| Local diagnosis | Modification index (score statistic; Lagrange multiplier) and expected parameter change (EPC; standardized EPC) | A local one-parameter approximation to the improvement from releasing one fixed restriction, with the approximate value the released parameter would take. Read with the residual pattern, the parameter's meaning, and the status of the search; not the exact LR change, and not an instruction. | Chapter 4, Sec. 6 |
| Comparison | Nested difference test ($\chi^2$ difference; likelihood-ratio difference test) | $\Delta T=T_R-T_U$ on $\Delta df=df_R-df_U$ for regularly nested, compatible ML fits on identical cases, outcomes, scale, mean structure, and likelihood convention. A smaller parameter count is not proof of nesting, and failure to reject is not equivalence. | Chapter 4, Sec. 4 |
| Comparison | Information criteria for covariance structures (AIC; BIC) eligibility | $-2\ell+2q$ and $-2\ell+q\log N$ with $q$ the effective free-parameter count. They rank eligible candidates fitted to the same observations and outcomes under one likelihood convention, including nonnested ones; neither is a test or an adequacy index. | Chapter 4, Sec. 4 |
| Comparison | Score, Wald, and likelihood-ratio views of one restriction | Three statistics for one null: slope and information at the restricted fit; distance of the unrestricted estimate from the restriction relative to its uncertainty; difference of optimized likelihoods. Asymptotic equivalence is not finite-sample equality. | Chapter 4, Sec. 4 |
| Comparison | Equivalent models (covariance-equivalent representation) | Distinct specifications with the same set of admissible implied covariance matrices, so that each is nested in the other: every covariance matrix one can reproduce, the other can also reproduce, as an exact parameter mapping shows. On any data they therefore give the same fitted covariance matrix, statistic, df, and fit indices. Identical fit in one sample is a consequence, not a test, and no covariance data can choose between them; only theory and evidence beyond reproduced covariance can. | Chapter 4, Sec. 5 |
| Extensions | Higher-order factor model (second-order factor; first-order disturbance) | A model in which one further latent variable accounts for the covariances among first-order factors, $\boldsymbol\Phi_l=\boldsymbol\gamma\boldsymbol\gamma^{\mathsf T}+\boldsymbol\Psi_h$. The first-order disturbances are distinct from indicator residuals. With diagonal first-order disturbances, the generic covariance-equality restriction count is $m(m-3)/2$ for $m\ge3$: three factors add no equality degrees of freedom, but nonnegative disturbance variances still restrict the admissible correlations. | Chapter 4, Sec. 5 |
| Extensions | Bifactor model (general plus orthogonal specific or group factors) | Every item loads directly on one general factor and one assigned specific factor, all factors mutually orthogonal. A specific factor is common variance among its items after the general factor is held constant, not an item residual, and the model is generally nonnested against a correlated-factor model of the same items. | Chapter 4, Sec. 5 |
| Extensions | Schmid-Leiman transformation and the proportionality restriction | The algebraic rewriting of a higher-order model as an orthogonal general factor with loadings $\boldsymbol\Lambda_l\boldsymbol\gamma$ and specific factors with loadings $\boldsymbol\Lambda_l\boldsymbol\Psi_h^{1/2}$. Because both come from one loading matrix, each simple-structure item in a domain has the same general-to-specific loading ratio $\gamma_k/\psi_{h,k}^{1/2}$; a freely estimated bifactor model is not bound by that ratio. | Chapter 4, Sec. 5 |
| Extensions | Method effect; testlet effect | Common variance among items sharing a format (reverse keying, response scale, informant) or a stimulus (passage, vignette, apparatus). Both are design-known groupings and the least controversial motivation for a specific factor, which generalizes a freed residual covariance to several items. | Chapter 4, Sec. 5 |
| Reliability | Cronbach's alpha for a declared unit-weighted score, $\alpha_C$ | A coefficient computed from item variances and their total-score variance. Interpreting it as reliability requires additional measurement assumptions; it is not a universal lower bound when residual dependence is allowed. | Chapter 4, Sec. 8 |
| Reliability | Model-based omega for a declared score, $\omega(\mathbf w)$ (composite reliability) | The proportion of a declared weighted composite's model-implied variance attributable to all modeled common factors. It retains cross-loadings, factor correlations, and modeled residual covariances, and is conditional on model, weights, and sample. | Chapter 4, Sec. 8 |
| Reliability | Omega-hierarchical, $\omega_h(\mathbf w)$ | The share of a declared score's variance attributable specifically to a bifactor general factor. Its complement within total omega is modeled reliable specific-factor variance, not error, and a substantial value does not establish essential unidimensionality. | Chapter 4, Sec. 5 |
| Reliability | Average variance extracted (AVE) and coefficient $H$ as bounded neighbours | AVE summarizes average communality for a simple fully-standardized single-factor item set; $H=a/(1+a)$ with $a=\boldsymbol\lambda^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\Theta^{-1}\boldsymbol\lambda$ is a maximum over optimally weighted composites. Neither is the reliability of a stated unit-weighted score, and neither applies unqualified to a cross-loading subscale. | Chapter 4, Appendix |
| Scores | Factor score (regression or conditional-mean score; Bartlett score) and factor-score determinacy | A model-dependent linear prediction of a latent variable from the indicators, whose weights use the whole fitted structure; determinacy is the model-based correlation between factor and prediction. A score is a prediction with nonzero conditional variance, not an observed latent value. | Chapter 4, Sec. 8 |
| Analytic history | Pseudo-true (population-ML) parameter and population discrepancy ($F_0$; population RMSEA) | The optimum of a misspecified model fitted to the exact generating covariance, and the discrepancy remaining there. Displacement at this optimum is deterministic under two stated specifications, not sampling fluctuation and not finite-sample estimator bias. | Chapter 4, Sec. 7 |
| Analytic history | Post-selection revision and independent revalidation | A change suggested by inspecting a body of evidence is exploratory with respect to that evidence, whatever function fits it; only records not used to suggest it can support it, and a retest that fails to support it does not prove the parameter is zero. | Chapter 4, Sec. 6 |

: Evaluation, comparison, reliability, and extensions. {#tbl-intro-p2-concepts-evaluation tbl-colwidths="[16,23,45,16]"}

\Needspace{18\baselineskip}

## Observed Structural Systems {#sec-p2-concepts-path .unnumbered}

| Concept group | Term and common alternatives | Meaning or essential distinction | Main explanation |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Structural systems | Structural equation | An equation representing an outcome as a function of its designated predictors and a disturbance, within a declared system. Its causal interpretation requires assumptions beyond covariance fit. | Chapter 5, Sec. 1 |
| Structural systems | Endogenous variable | A variable explained by another variable in the structural system. This model role differs from econometric endogeneity, which concerns dependence between a regressor and its equation's disturbance. | Chapter 5, Sec. 1; Sec. 3 |
| Structural systems | Exogenous variable | A variable whose distribution is supplied without modeling incoming structural paths in the declared system. The label alone does not establish independence from every unmeasured cause. | Chapter 5, Sec. 1 |
| Structural systems | Structural disturbance ($\zeta$) | Variation in a structural outcome not represented by its designated predictors. Covariances among disturbances and with exogenous variables are part of the model's assumptions. | Chapter 5, Sec. 1 |
| Structural systems | Reduced form | The structural equations solved in terms of the exogenous inputs and disturbances, when the required inverse exists. Reduced-form coefficients combine direct and transmitted relationships. | Chapter 5, Sec. 1; Sec. 7 |
| Structural systems | Direct, indirect and total effect | A direct coefficient belongs to one structural equation; an indirect contribution follows a directed route. In an acyclic linear system, the total sums the compatible directed-route products. Feedback requires the inverse-system response. A causal reading requires the declared causal assumptions. | Chapter 5, Sec. 2; Sec. 7 |
| Structural systems | Saturated structural system | A structural parameterization that leaves the modeled variables' covariance unrestricted. Its coefficients can be estimated with uncertainty even though its global covariance test has zero degrees of freedom. | Chapter 5, Sec. 3; Sec. 4 |
| Structural systems | Recursive and nonrecursive system | Under the chapter's convention, a recursive linear system has an acyclic ordering, mutually uncorrelated disturbances, and disturbances uncorrelated with exogenous inputs. Feedback or relaxed disturbance assumptions require a separate identification analysis. | Chapter 5, Sec. 1; Sec. 7 |
| Feedback | Feedback (reciprocal system) | A directed cycle in a simultaneous structural system. Its equilibrium interpretation differs from an observed lagged relationship across measurement occasions. | Chapter 5, Sec. 7 |
| Feedback | Equilibrium stability | For the declared repeated linear adjustment, the condition $\rho(\mathbf B)<1$ that makes departures decay. Existence of $(\mathbf I-\mathbf B)^{-1}$ alone does not establish stability. | Chapter 5, Sec. 7 |
| Reproducibility | Summary-statistic reconstruction | Analysis using the published moments, variable definitions, sample information and model restrictions actually available. Distinguish a numerical reproduction from a changed reanalysis or an independent empirical replication. | Chapter 5, Sec. 5; Sec. 8 |

: Observed Structural Systems. {#tbl-intro-p2-concepts-path tbl-colwidths="[14,22,48,16]"}

\Needspace{18\baselineskip}

## Causal Models, Interventions and Identification {#sec-p2-concepts-causal .unnumbered}

| Concept group | Term and common alternatives | Meaning or essential distinction | Main explanation |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Causal interpretation | Structural causal model (SCM) | Structural assignments and a distribution for their disturbances, with an intervention defined by replacing an assignment while retaining the other declared mechanisms. | Chapter 6, Sec. 1 |
| Causal interpretation | Conditioning | Comparing or selecting observations at a recorded value of a variable. It generally changes the distribution of related variables and is different from intervening on the variable. | Chapter 6, Sec. 1 |
| Causal interpretation | Intervention | Replacing a variable's structural assignment by a specified value or policy under the model's invariance assumptions. Setting a value removes that variable's incoming causal arrows. | Chapter 6, Sec. 4 |
| Causal interpretation | Collider | A variable at which two arrows on a path meet head to head. Conditioning on it or its descendant can open an otherwise blocked path. | Chapter 6, Sec. 2 |
| Causal interpretation | d-separation | A graph criterion that blocks every path between two sets under a conditioning set and implies conditional independence under the graph's Markov assumptions. An open path permits dependence but does not guarantee it for every parameter value. | Chapter 6, Sec. 2 |
| Identification | Instrumental variable | A source of regressor variation requiring relevance, exclusion from the outcome equation, and the stated independence or orthogonality to its disturbance. A first-stage association tests neither exclusion nor exogeneity. | Chapter 6, Sec. 6 |
| Identification | Instrument relevance | Association with the endogenous regressor after the included controls are accounted for. Weak conditional association makes the identifying covariance ratio unstable. | Chapter 6, Sec. 6 |
| Identification | Exclusion restriction | A restriction removing a direct route from an instrument to the outcome in the stated structural equation and control set. It needs substantive support distinct from first-stage strength. | Chapter 6, Sec. 6 |
| Identification | Causal identification | Whether the stated causal target is uniquely determined by the observed distribution together with the declared causal assumptions; statistical parameter recovery within one chosen model does not establish this. | Chapter 6, Sec. 1; Sec. 6 |
| Adjustment | Backdoor adjustment | Recovering an intervention distribution by averaging conditional outcome distributions over a stated target covariate distribution when the covariates satisfy the causal adjustment requirements, with consistency and positivity. | Chapter 6, Sec. 4 |
| Counterfactuals | Counterfactual outcome | The outcome under a specified replacement of a structural assignment while retaining the unit's relevant disturbances; factual evidence determines what is known or uncertain about those disturbances. | Chapter 6, Sec. 5 |
| Counterfactuals | Abduction, action and prediction | Updating disturbance information using factual evidence, replacing the specified assignment, and propagating that retained information through the altered system. | Chapter 6, Sec. 5 |
| Sensitivity | Exclusion sensitivity | Re-estimating a target under explicitly fixed alternative direct instrument-outcome effects; conditional sampling intervals and the across-assumption sensitivity range answer different questions. | Chapter 6, Sec. 7 |

: Causal Models, Interventions and Identification. {#tbl-intro-p2-concepts-causal tbl-colwidths="[14,22,48,16]"}

\Needspace{18\baselineskip}

## Joint Measurement and Structural Modeling {#sec-p2-concepts-sem .unnumbered}

| Concept group | Term and common alternatives | Meaning or essential distinction | Main explanation |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Full SEM | Joint measurement model | One model containing all relevant measurement blocks, with their factors allowed to covary before structural restrictions are imposed. | Chapter 7, Sec. 1 |
| Full SEM | Two-step SEM workflow | Evaluation of a joint measurement specification followed by joint estimation of its measurement and structural parameters in the full SEM. | Chapter 7, Sec. 1 |
| Full SEM | Structurally saturated model | A model whose structural component reproduces an unrestricted covariance among its latent variables; measurement restrictions may still leave the complete model with positive degrees of freedom. | Chapter 7, Sec. 2; Sec. 4 |
| Exploratory measurement | ESEM | A structural equation model containing an exploratory factor block whose estimated loadings are oriented by rotation, potentially alongside confirmatory blocks and structural regressions. | Chapter 7, Sec. 5 |
| Exploratory measurement | Target rotation | Rotation toward a declared loading pattern whose target entries guide orientation rather than necessarily fixing corresponding loadings to exact values. | Chapter 7, Sec. 5 |
| Measurement representation | Causal indicator | An observed variable proposed to contribute to a latent variable whose disturbance represents additional causes. Identification requires more than assigning arrows to its predictors. | Chapter 7, Sec. 6 |
| Measurement representation | Exact composite | A variable defined as a specified weighted combination of observed components, with no disturbance in that defining equation. | Chapter 7, Sec. 6 |
| Means and covariates | Mean structure | The model's specification of expected observed levels through intercepts, latent means, and predictor means. | Chapter 7, Sec. 7 |
| Means and covariates | MIMIC model | A model combining observed predictors of a latent variable with multiple indicators of that latent variable. | Chapter 7, Sec. 7 |

: Joint Measurement and Structural Modeling. {#tbl-intro-p2-concepts-sem tbl-colwidths="[14,22,48,16]"}

\Needspace{18\baselineskip}

## Indirect and Conditional Relationships {#sec-p2-concepts-conditional .unnumbered}

| Concept group | Term and common alternatives | Meaning or essential distinction | Main explanation |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Indirect relationships | Specific indirect effect | The product of coefficients along one directed indirect route between a stated source and outcome in the declared linear structural system. | Chapter 8, Sec. 1 |
| Indirect relationships | Total indirect effect | The sum of the specified directed indirect-route contributions between the same source and outcome. Contributions with opposite signs can cancel. | Chapter 8, Sec. 2 |
| Indirect relationships | Indirect-effect contrast | A difference or other declared comparison of indirect effects whose uncertainty retains the dependence between their estimated component paths. | Chapter 8, Sec. 2 |
| Conditional relationships | Conditional slope | The rate of change in a modeled conditional mean with a predictor at stated values of the moderator and other conditioned variables. Its value depends on the declared scale and origin. | Chapter 8, Sec. 6 |
| Conditional relationships | Latent interaction | A product relationship involving latent predictors represented through explicit measurement models. A latent outcome alone does not turn an observed predictor product into a latent interaction. | Chapter 8, Sec. 5 |
| Conditional relationships | Product indicator | An observed product of indicators used to represent a latent product under specified measurement-error and centering assumptions. Its measurement error contains more than the product of the two original errors. | Chapter 8, Sec. 5 |
| Conditional relationships | Conditional indirect effect | A specified indirect-effect function evaluated at stated moderator values, with its uncertainty propagated through the joint parameter estimates. | Chapter 8, Sec. 7 |
| Conditional relationships | Index of moderated mediation | The coefficient describing change in a specified indirect effect per unit of a moderator when that indirect-effect function is linear in the moderator. Its formula depends on the structural model. | Chapter 8, Sec. 7 |

: Indirect and Conditional Relationships. {#tbl-intro-p2-concepts-conditional tbl-colwidths="[14,22,48,16]"}

\Needspace{18\baselineskip}

## Measurement Comparability and Group Comparisons {#sec-p2-concepts-comparability .unnumbered}

| Concept group | Term and common alternatives | Meaning or essential distinction | Main explanation |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Comparability | Measurement invariance | Equality of the conditional response distribution across groups at the same latent values. Particular loading, intercept and residual restrictions express aspects of this requirement within a declared measurement model. | Chapter 9, Sec. 1; Sec. 3 |
| Comparability | Configural model | A joint group model with the same designated factor-loading pattern and separately estimated group parameters under declared scale and location constraints. The shared pattern alone does not establish a common factor unit or origin. | Chapter 9, Sec. 2 |
| Comparability | Metric invariance (loading invariance) | Equality of the designated factor loadings across groups, supporting a common factor unit through the stated anchors. It does not impose common indicator intercepts or residual structures. | Chapter 9, Sec. 3 |
| Comparability | Scalar invariance (intercept invariance) | Equality of the designated indicator intercepts as well as loadings, supporting a common origin for the specified latent-mean comparison. The comparison group's latent means remain free when they are the target. | Chapter 9, Sec. 3 |
| Comparability | Strict invariance | Equality of the measurement residual covariance structure in addition to the scalar restrictions. It is not generally required for a latent-mean comparison and does not alone guarantee equal reliability. | Chapter 9, Sec. 3 |
| Comparability | Partial invariance | A declared model that retains specified cross-group equality restrictions while allowing selected measurement parameters to differ. Its interpretation depends on the remaining anchors and the evidence supporting them. | Chapter 9, Sec. 4 |
| Identification and comparison | Anchor | A retained measurement restriction that supplies a common reference for the latent scale or origin. A numerically identifying anchor can still lack substantive comparability. | Chapter 9, Sec. 4 |
| Identification and comparison | Anchor sensitivity | Variation in an interpreted factor comparison when the declared parameters linking its scale or origin across groups are changed. | Chapter 9, Sec. 4 |
| Group targets | Latent-mean contrast | A difference or other declared comparison of latent means on a supported common scale and origin. Its standardized form additionally depends on the chosen reference variance. | Chapter 9, Sec. 5 |
| Group targets | Multigroup SEM | Joint estimation of group-specific measurement and structural systems with explicit restrictions on which parameters are shared and which can differ. | Chapter 9, Sec. 2; Sec. 5 |
| Group targets | Conditional group contrast | A comparison at specified covariate values under the fitted model. It can differ from the marginal group difference because the groups' covariate distributions differ. | Chapter 9, Sec. 5; Sec. 6 |
| Item comparisons | Intercept differential item functioning (uniform DIF) | A group difference in an indicator's conditional expected response at the same latent values, represented by an intercept difference or a group-to-indicator direct path in the stated model. It is distinct from loading noninvariance. | Chapter 9, Sec. 6 |

: Measurement Comparability and Group Comparisons. {#tbl-intro-p2-concepts-comparability tbl-colwidths="[14,22,48,16]"}

\Needspace{18\baselineskip}

## Incomplete Data and Robust Inference {#sec-p2-concepts-missing .unnumbered}

| Concept group | Term and common alternatives | Meaning or essential distinction | Main explanation |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Observation process | Missingness pattern | The combination of observed and missing variables in a record. | Chapter 10, Sec. 1 |
| Observation process | MCAR | Missingness does not depend on the observed or unobserved values in the analysis. | Chapter 10, Sec. 2 |
| Observation process | MAR | Conditional on the observed information included in the analysis, missingness does not depend on the unobserved values. | Chapter 10, Sec. 2 |
| Observation process | MNAR | Missingness still depends on unobserved values after conditioning on the observed information in the analysis. | Chapter 10, Sec. 2 |
| Observation process | Ignorability | Conditions under which inference for the data-model parameters can omit an explicit missingness model; for likelihood inference these include MAR and distinct parameters. | Chapter 10, Sec. 2 |
| Observed-data estimation | Observed-data likelihood | A likelihood formed from the values actually observed, integrating over the missing values under the specified model. | Chapter 10, Sec. 3 |
| Observed-data estimation | FIML | Joint maximum-likelihood estimation using each record's observed variables and the corresponding model-implied distribution. | Chapter 10, Sec. 3 |
| Additional information | Auxiliary variable | An additional variable included to supply information about incomplete values or missingness without assigning it a substantive structural role. | Chapter 10, Sec. 6 |
| Robust inference | Sandwich covariance | A parameter covariance estimate combining likelihood curvature with the empirical variability of individual score contributions. | Chapter 10, Sec. 5 |
| Robust inference | Scaled difference test | A model-comparison test that adjusts the difference in compatible unscaled fit statistics using information from the fitted models. | Chapter 10, Sec. 5 |
| Additional information | Sensitivity parameter | A quantity fixed at substantively considered values to examine how conclusions depend on an assumption the observed data do not identify. | Chapter 10, Sec. 6 |

: Incomplete Data and Robust Inference. {#tbl-intro-p2-concepts-missing tbl-colwidths="[14,22,48,16]"}

\Needspace{18\baselineskip}

## Latent Growth Models {#sec-p2-concepts-growth .unnumbered}

| Concept group | Term and common alternatives | Meaning or essential distinction | Main explanation |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Trajectory components | Latent intercept | A person-specific level of the modeled trajectory at the declared time origin. Its unit and location depend on the outcome or measurement scale. | Chapter 11, Sec. 2 |
| Trajectory components | Latent slope | A person-specific change per unit of coded time in a linear growth model; its meaning changes when the time unit or growth basis changes. | Chapter 11, Sec. 2 |
| Trajectory components | Mean slope | The population mean of the latent slope in an unconditional model; with predictors, the structural slope intercept describes the mean at the stated predictor reference. | Chapter 11, Sec. 2 |
| Trajectory components | Slope variance | Between-person variance of the latent slope under the specified trajectory model, distinct from uncertainty in the estimated mean slope. | Chapter 11, Sec. 2 |
| Time and shape | Intercept–slope covariance | Covariance between the latent level at a declared time origin and the latent slope; changing that origin can change its value or sign without changing the modeled trajectories. | Chapter 11, Sec. 4 |
| Time and shape | Time centering | Replacing time by time minus a stated constant, changing the intercept meaning and its moments while preserving the same trajectory model. | Chapter 11, Sec. 4 |
| Time and shape | Latent basis | A growth model that fixes two basis loadings to set the origin and unit and estimates the remaining loadings; people share the basis shape while their levels and amplitudes vary. | Chapter 11, Sec. 4 |
| Time and shape | Piecewise growth | A trajectory represented by distinct functions over prespecified time segments, with explicit restrictions on the knot, continuity and the meaning of each slope. | Chapter 11, Sec. 4 |
| Longitudinal measurement | Occasion disturbance | An occasion-specific latent deviation from the growth curve, distinguished from an indicator-specific measurement residual in a multiple-indicator growth model. | Chapter 11, Sec. 5 |
| Longitudinal measurement | Longitudinal measurement comparability | Support for measurement restrictions that make the intended construct comparison meaningful across occasions, including suitable loading and intercept anchors for latent mean growth. | Chapter 11, Sec. 5 |

: Latent Growth Models. {#tbl-intro-p2-concepts-growth tbl-colwidths="[14,22,48,16]"}

\Needspace{18\baselineskip}

## Study Planning and Power Analysis {#sec-p2-concepts-planning .unnumbered}

| Concept group | Term and common alternatives | Meaning or essential distinction | Main explanation |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Study planning | Prospective power | Probability that a specified test rejects its null under a stated alternative, study design and analysis. | Chapter 12, Secs. 1 and 3 |
| Study planning | Parameter power | Power for a named parameter restriction within a specified model. | Chapter 12, Secs. 1 and 3 |
| Study planning | Global-fit power | Power for a stated hypothesis about the model's overall population discrepancy. | Chapter 12, Sec. 3 |
| Study planning | Calibration scenario | A fully specified planning population informed by evidence and explicit choices. | Chapter 12, Sec. 2 |
| Simulation | Monte Carlo error | Numerical uncertainty because performance is estimated from finitely many simulated studies. | Chapter 12, Sec. 5 |
| Simulation | Operating characteristic | A feature of an analysis's repeated-study performance under a declared scenario. | Chapter 12, Sec. 5 |
| Simulation | Coverage | Probability that the stated interval procedure contains the target value across repeated studies under the scenario. | Chapter 12, Sec. 5 |
| Simulation | Simulation failure rate | Fraction of scheduled analysis attempts that fail the declared convergence, admissibility or usable-output criteria. | Chapter 12, Sec. 5 |
| Study planning | Precision target | A declared requirement for the uncertainty of the study's estimate. | Chapter 12, Secs. 1 and 8 |

: Study Planning and Power Analysis. {#tbl-intro-p2-concepts-planning tbl-colwidths="[14,22,48,16]"}
